zanamivir-pharmacology-safety.title: Verify the Zanamivir Device and Airway
zanamivir-pharmacology-safety.summary: Link inhaled neuraminidase inhibition to the labeled two-blister dose, demonstrated Diskhaler technique, airway and ingredient screening, and the separate treatment, prophylaxis and live-vaccine calendars.
zanamivir-pharmacology-safety.application: Verify the indication, full two-inhalation dose and demonstrated delivery, then distinguish an airway warning, a true ingredient-allergy contraindication and a live-vaccine timing interaction.

lesson.heading: Build the labeled treatment dose
lesson.body: Zanamivir inhibits influenza neuraminidase, limiting release of viral particles from infected cells and their spread in the respiratory tract. Relenza is labeled for uncomplicated influenza A or B in patients aged 7 years and older who have been symptomatic for no more than two days. Treatment is 10 mg twice daily for five days, with each dose delivered as two separate 5 mg blister inhalations through the supplied Diskhaler. Give two doses on the first day when possible, at least two hours apart; subsequent doses are approximately 12 hours apart. The labeled dose uses the blister strength, not an independently estimated amount deposited in the airway. Priority-patient treatment decisions and later presentation require the separate clinical selection assessment.

lesson.heading: Keep prophylaxis calendars distinct
lesson.body: The book and Relenza label describe 10 mg once daily for prophylaxis: ten days after household exposure in adults and children aged 5 years and older, or 28 days during a community outbreak in adults and adolescents. Current CDC guidance instead describes seven days after the last known exposure for ordinary chemoprophylaxis. For institutional outbreaks, CDC recommends at least two weeks, continuing up to one week after the last known case is identified. Identify whether the plan follows a labeled household or community regimen or a CDC exposure or outbreak protocol, including its starting and stopping clock. Do not interchange treatment’s twice-daily schedule with prophylaxis’s once-daily schedule, or apply the adult/adolescent community regimen to every child simply because the general prophylaxis indication begins at age 5. The label states that prophylaxis efficacy has not been proven in the nursing-home setting; keep that evidence limitation distinct from CDC’s institutional outbreak recommendation.

lesson.heading: Load and pierce the Rotadisk
lesson.body: Demonstrate the supplied device and have the patient or caregiver show the steps. Remove the blue cover and check that the mouthpiece is clear. Pull out the white tray, press its side ridges to remove it, place the Rotadisk on the wheel with its flat side up and the four blisters fitted underneath, and slide the tray fully back in. Keep the Diskhaler level. Only when ready to inhale, raise the piercing flap fully upright to pierce the upper and lower foil of the positioned blister, then close the flap. A partly raised flap or pierced blister stored for later does not demonstrate correct preparation.

lesson.heading: Deliver both inhalations
lesson.body: Exhale before placing the mouthpiece in the mouth, keeping exhaled air away from the powder. Seal the lips around the mouthpiece without covering its side air holes, inhale steadily and deeply through the mouth, and hold the breath for a few seconds. Pull the tray out and push it back without removing it to advance to the next blister; pierce and inhale again to finish the second 5 mg inhalation. Replace the cover afterward. One four-blister Rotadisk supplies two complete 10 mg doses. A standard five-day twice-daily treatment course therefore uses ten doses, or twenty blisters, equal to five Rotadisks. Assess device ability and inspiratory delivery rather than assuming age eligibility proves successful use; children need supervision by an adult trained in the device.

lesson.heading: Preserve the labeled route and device
lesson.body: Relenza inhalation powder is administered by oral inhalation only through the supplied Diskhaler. Do not prepare an improvised solution for a nebulizer or mechanical ventilation. The label describes a fatal report in which lactose from such a solution obstructed equipment. A patient who cannot operate the device or deliver the inhalation needs assessment of another suitable antiviral route; converting this powder into an intravenous, nasal or nebulized preparation is not an administration workaround.

lesson.heading: Protect vulnerable airways
lesson.body: Zanamivir is not recommended for treatment or prophylaxis in people with underlying airway disease such as asthma or COPD because of serious bronchospasm risk. Serious and fatal bronchospasm has also been reported without a prior airway history; postmarketing reports do not establish the drug’s contribution in every case. Stop Relenza for bronchospasm or declining respiratory function and obtain immediate treatment; hospital care may be required. If a clinician nevertheless considers use in underlying airway disease, the label calls for weighing benefit and risk, close monitoring and appropriate support including a fast-acting inhaled bronchodilator. When a scheduled inhaled bronchodilator is taken at the same time, administer it before Relenza. Bronchodilator availability or sequence does not remove the warning or make zanamivir the routine asthma choice.

lesson.heading: Identify true ingredient allergy
lesson.body: The lactose vehicle contains milk proteins. A history of an allergic reaction to any Relenza ingredient, including milk proteins, is a contraindication. Milk-protein allergy differs from digestive lactose intolerance; neither a digestive symptom alone nor a sugar-free preference establishes the contraindication. Clarify the reaction and exact product ingredients rather than guaranteeing suitability from a vague intolerance history. Allergic reactions including oropharyngeal swelling, serious skin reactions and anaphylaxis have been reported. Stop treatment and provide appropriate care if an allergic reaction develops or is suspected.

lesson.heading: Separate the live-vaccine intervals
lesson.body: Zanamivir may interfere with replication of live attenuated influenza vaccine virus. Unless medically indicated, do not give zanamivir until at least two weeks after intranasal LAIV, and do not give LAIV until at least 48 hours after zanamivir has been stopped. The latter interval starts after the final dose, not the first dose of a continuing course. The Relenza label permits trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine at any time relative to the drug. Antiviral use does not replace seasonal influenza vaccination.

lesson.heading: Monitor symptoms without assuming their cause
lesson.body: The book lists headache, throat pain and cough among zanamivir adverse effects. Trial reactions must be interpreted in context: both Relenza and placebo groups inhaled lactose vehicle, and a new cough with worsening breathing requires the airway warning response rather than routine reassurance. Influenza itself can cause seizures, hallucinations, delirium and abnormal behavior. Neuropsychiatric events have been reported during neuraminidase-inhibitor treatment, primarily in children; the drug’s contribution is not established and voluntary reports cannot supply a reliable frequency. Closely monitor behavior, report confusion, seizures or hallucinations promptly to the clinician, and assess continuation benefits and risks individually. Relenza has not been shown to prevent bacterial complications; persistent or worsening illness needs reassessment for coexisting or secondary infection.

keyPoints: One 10 mg dose requires two separate 5 mg inhalations through the supplied Diskhaler.
Keep treatment, labeled prophylaxis and CDC exposure-based calendars distinct.
Avoid routine zanamivir selection in asthma or COPD; stop for bronchospasm or respiratory decline.
True ingredient allergy is a contraindication; time LAIV from the relevant vaccine date or final antiviral dose.

check.question: Why should a patient with asthma usually receive an alternative to zanamivir?
choices: Zanamivir can cause serious bronchospasm
Asthma prevents influenza infection
The drug is renally toxic in every patient
The Diskhaler contains an antibiotic
check.rationale: Serious bronchospasm risk makes zanamivir not recommended in underlying airway disease such as asthma. Asthma does not prevent influenza infection. The label does not claim renal toxicity in every patient, and the Diskhaler delivers an antiviral rather than an antibiotic.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-097.question: Which statement correctly links zanamivir’s antiviral target and its labeled delivery?
choices: It inhibits influenza neuraminidase and is inhaled orally through the supplied Diskhaler
It inhibits neuraminidase and its Diskhaler powder can be nebulized interchangeably
It inhibits the M2 channel and is swallowed as a Relenza tablet
It inhibits the PA endonuclease and is given as an intravenous Relenza push
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-097.rationale: Zanamivir inhibits neuraminidase and uses the supplied oral-inhalation device. Nebulization of this powder is prohibited; M2 and PA endonuclease are different targets, and Relenza is neither a tablet nor an intravenous push.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-098.question: Which preparation demonstrates correct Rotadisk placement and piercing?
choices: Place the flat side up, keep the device level and fully raise then close the piercing flap when ready
Place the flat side down and inhale before piercing any foil
Pierce all four blisters in advance and store them open for later doses
Raise the flap only partway so the lower foil stays intact
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-098.rationale: The flat side faces up with blisters underneath; the level device and fully raised flap allow both foil surfaces to be pierced just before use. The alternatives invert placement, omit piercing, prepare blisters prematurely or leave preparation incomplete.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-099.question: A trained caregiver is showing a child how to finish a zanamivir dose. Which demonstration is correct?
choices: Exhale away, inhale through the mouthpiece with side holes clear, then advance and repeat with a second blister
Exhale into the loaded mouthpiece to disperse the powder before inhaling
Cover both side air holes tightly and inhale through the nose
Use one blister and count it as the complete 10 mg dose
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-099.rationale: The technique requires mouth inhalation with open side holes and two separately prepared blisters. Exhaling into the device, blocking airflow or inhaling nasally is incorrect; one blister supplies only 5 mg of the labeled 10 mg dose.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-100.question: An age-eligible child cannot demonstrate effective Diskhaler use. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Assess device ability, trained adult supervision and another suitable antiviral route if delivery remains inadequate
Assume age eligibility guarantees effective inspiratory delivery
Dissolve the powder for a nebulizer as a routine substitution
Prescribe additional blisters without evaluating technique
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-100.rationale: Eligibility alone does not establish delivery. Demonstration and trained adult supervision are required considerations; persistent inability calls for a suitable alternative. Nebulizing the powder is prohibited, and extra blisters do not correct an unassessed device problem.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-101.question: Which regimen matches labeled zanamivir treatment of uncomplicated influenza in an eligible patient aged 7 years or older?
choices: 10 mg by two separate 5 mg inhalations twice daily for five days
One 5 mg inhalation twice daily for five days
10 mg by two inhalations once daily as the treatment schedule
10 mg once by intravenous push
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-101.rationale: Treatment is two 5 mg inhalations per 10 mg dose, twice daily for five days. One blister underfills the labeled dose; once daily is a prophylaxis frequency, and intravenous push is not the labeled Relenza route.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-102.question: When two zanamivir treatment doses are possible on the first day, which spacing matches the label?
choices: At least two hours apart on day one, then approximately twelve hours apart on later days
Both doses at the same moment on day one, then approximately twelve hours apart
At least two hours apart for every subsequent twice-daily dose throughout the course
One dose on day one followed by a mandatory skipped second day
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-102.rationale: The label allows two first-day doses at least two hours apart, followed by approximately twelve-hour spacing. Simultaneous dosing, perpetuating a two-hour interval or inventing a skipped day does not match that schedule.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-103.question: Which calculation correctly converts the standard five-day twice-daily zanamivir treatment course into blisters?
choices: Ten complete doses require twenty 5 mg blisters
Ten complete doses require ten 5 mg blisters
Five complete doses require twenty 5 mg blisters
Twenty complete doses require ten 5 mg blisters
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-103.rationale: Two doses daily for five days gives ten doses; each uses two blisters, so twenty are required. Ten blisters supplies only five doses, while the other alternatives mismatch dose and blister counts.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-104.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes zanamivir prophylaxis durations?
choices: The label’s household course is ten days, while CDC ordinary prophylaxis runs seven days after the last known exposure
The labeled ten-day household course and CDC seven-day course use an identical duration and stopping clock
The 28-day labeled community regimen applies automatically to every child aged 5 or older
All prophylaxis regimens use the treatment frequency of twice daily
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-104.rationale: The labeled household duration and CDC last-exposure duration need distinct context and clocks. They are not identical. The community label regimen is described for adults/adolescents, and prophylaxis is once daily rather than the treatment frequency.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-105.question: How should asthma or COPD affect routine selection of inhaled zanamivir?
choices: Choose another suitable antiviral because zanamivir is not recommended in underlying airway disease
Choose zanamivir routinely because asthma improves inspiratory drug delivery
Ignore the airway history if the two-blister dose is calculated correctly
Treat bronchodilator possession as proof that the warning no longer applies
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-105.rationale: The airway warning supports another suitable antiviral. Asthma does not establish improved delivery; correct dose arithmetic and possession of a bronchodilator do not remove bronchospasm risk.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-106.question: A patient develops bronchospasm and declining respiratory function during Relenza treatment. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Stop Relenza and obtain immediate respiratory treatment, with hospital care if needed
Continue every remaining dose before assessing the decline
Double the next dose to overcome the bronchospasm
Convert the same powder into a mechanical-ventilation solution
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-106.rationale: The label directs discontinuation and immediate treatment for bronchospasm or respiratory decline. Continuing without assessment or increasing the dose is not warning management, and an improvised ventilation solution is prohibited.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-107.question: If a clinician has selected Relenza and a scheduled inhaled bronchodilator is taken at the same time, what instruction matches the label?
choices: Give the bronchodilator before Relenza while retaining the airway-risk assessment and monitoring
Give Relenza first because the bronchodilator blocks neuraminidase inhibition
Mix both medicines into a single nebulized Relenza solution
Use the sequence as proof Relenza is routinely recommended in asthma
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-107.rationale: The scheduled bronchodilator goes first. This instruction does not cancel the airway warning. The alternatives reverse the labeled sequence, invent a mixing route or falsely make asthma a routine indication.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-108.question: Which interpretation of Relenza bronchospasm reports is accurate?
choices: Serious events have occurred with and without prior airway disease, and each report does not prove drug causality
Patients without known airway disease have no possible bronchospasm risk
Every postmarketing report provides definite proof that zanamivir caused the event
A report’s uncertain causality permits respiratory decline to be ignored
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-108.rationale: The warning includes both airway-history groups and qualifies postmarketing causality. Absence of prior disease is not immunity, a report is not certain causal proof, and uncertainty never justifies ignoring respiratory decline.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-109.question: Which history meets the Relenza ingredient-allergy contraindication?
choices: A prior allergic reaction to milk proteins contained in the lactose vehicle
Digestive symptoms after lactose without an allergic reaction history
A preference for less sweet medicines without allergy
A question about whether the device has a lactose vehicle
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-109.rationale: An allergic reaction to an ingredient, including milk proteins, is contraindicated. Digestive intolerance requires clarification but is not identical to milk-protein allergy; taste preference and an ingredient question alone do not establish allergy.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-110.question: A patient says “I am lactose intolerant” when Relenza is being considered. What is the best response?
choices: Clarify digestive intolerance versus true milk-protein allergy and review the exact ingredients
Automatically diagnose anaphylactic milk allergy from that statement alone
Guarantee safety without asking about the prior reaction
Explain that Relenza contains no milk proteins
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-110.rationale: Clarify the reaction because lactose intolerance and milk-protein allergy differ. Neither automatically assigning anaphylaxis nor guaranteeing suitability is justified. The lactose vehicle does contain milk proteins.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-111.question: Unless medically indicated, how should intranasal LAIV be timed around a zanamivir course?
choices: Wait at least two weeks after LAIV before zanamivir and at least 48 hours after the final zanamivir dose before LAIV
Wait 48 hours after the first zanamivir dose before LAIV even while the course continues
Give zanamivir immediately after LAIV because antiviral activity improves live vaccine replication
Apply the same mandatory intervals to trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-111.rationale: The label specifies the two-week vaccine-before-drug interval and 48 hours after cessation for vaccine-after-drug timing. Counting from the first dose is wrong; antiviral activity may interfere with live vaccine replication. Trivalent inactivated vaccine can be given at any time relative to Relenza.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-112.question: A patient develops oropharyngeal swelling and a suspected allergic skin reaction during Relenza treatment. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Stop Relenza and provide appropriate care for the suspected allergic reaction
Continue and manage the swelling only by changing the blister order
Assume the reaction is harmless digestive lactose intolerance
Nebulize the remaining powder to avoid the allergy
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-112.rationale: Suspected allergic reactions require stopping and appropriate treatment. Blister order does not treat allergy, swelling is not ordinary digestive intolerance, and nebulizing the powder is prohibited and does not remove its ingredients.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-184.question: A patient with asthma asks for inhaled zanamivir. What is the best response?
choices: Choose another antiviral because of bronchospasm risk
Use zanamivir because asthma improves inhalation
Nebulize the Diskhaler powder
Double the first dose
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-184.rationale: Choose another suitable antiviral because Relenza is not recommended in underlying airway disease. Asthma does not improve inhalation safety; nebulizing the Diskhaler powder is prohibited, and doubling the dose does not address bronchospasm risk.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-185.question: How is one 10 mg zanamivir dose delivered?
choices: Two separate 5 mg Diskhaler inhalations
One 10 mg tablet
One 10 mg intravenous push
Four 2.5 mg nasal sprays
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-185.rationale: Each labeled 10 mg dose uses two separate 5 mg blisters inhaled orally through the supplied Diskhaler. The labeled Relenza product is not administered as a tablet, an intravenous push or nasal sprays.
